summary: Specifies RObust Header Compression, a framework and four profiles that compress headers of RTP/UDP/IP, UDP/IP, ESP/IP and uncompressed packets, built to cope with lossy links such as wireless. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: ROHC reduces repeated information in packet headers so more of a limited link can carry useful data. It also checks whether the receiver can rebuild each header, and provides ways to restore shared information after errors or lost packets.

why does crtp fail on cellular links
subtitle: A header compression framework designed to keep packet streams recoverable over lossy, high-latency links.

tldr.problem: RTP packets can carry 40 octets of IPv4, UDP and RTP headers for a speech payload of only 15 to 20 octets. Earlier compression schemes could lose many following packets when a lossy link and slow feedback left the decompressor with an out-of-date context.
tldr.mechanism: ROHC keeps matching contexts at the compressor and decompressor. It sends full initialization information, then uses sequence numbers, predicted field changes, checksums and optional feedback to send shorter headers and detect or repair context errors.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3095 defines four profiles for uncompressed packets, RTP/UDP/IP, UDP/IP and ESP/IP. It is a Proposed Standard and was updated by RFC 3759 and RFC 4815.

today: RFC 3095 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 3759 and RFC 4815. The unit metadata does not list an RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Headers Need Shrinking
sections.content:
RFC 3095 defines RObust Header Compression (ROHC), a framework for reducing packet headers on links where bandwidth is limited and errors are common. The main example is Internet voice traffic carried by the Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP), the User Datagram Protocol (UDP) and the Internet Protocol (IP).

An RTP packet over IPv4 has 20 octets of IP header, 8 octets of UDP header and 12 octets of RTP header: 40 octets in total. With IPv6, the headers total 60 octets. The speech data can be only 15 to 20 octets, so the headers can be larger than the payload.

The RFC describes cellular links with bit error rates up to 1e-3, or 1e-2 in severe conditions, and round-trip times up to 100 to 200 milliseconds. ROHC aims to reduce header overhead without letting a lost or damaged packet disrupt a long run of later packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Voice packets can carry more addressing information than speech data. ROHC shortens repeated header information to save bandwidth on links where packets can be lost or damaged.

sections.title: Why Earlier Compression Fell Short
sections.content:
Headers in one packet stream often repeat the same values or change in predictable ways. A compressor can send stable information once and let the receiver rebuild it from a shared context, the information both ends remember about that stream. If their contexts differ, the receiver may rebuild a wrong header or be unable to decode later packets.

The RFC explains that Compressed RTP (CRTP) could reduce IPv4/UDP/RTP headers to 2 octets when the UDP checksum was disabled, but it relied on feedback to repair a damaged context. On links with long round-trip times, packets could continue to be lost while that repair was pending. ROHC therefore seeks greater robustness without increasing the size of the shortest compressed headers.

Most header fields change rarely. The RFC identifies the IPv4 Identification field, UDP checksum, RTP marker bit, RTP sequence number and RTP timestamp as fields needing more careful handling. ROHC learns how changing fields relate to the sequence number and sends updates when those patterns change.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver remember information from earlier packets so they can avoid sending it again. If that remembered information gets out of step, later packets can be affected, so ROHC includes checks and repair methods.

sections.title: Contexts, States and Modes
sections.content:
ROHC creates a context for each packet stream. A context stores header values and patterns that help the compressor shorten later headers and help the decompressor rebuild them. A context identifier (CID) selects the context; the CID space belongs to one channel, so the same CID on another channel can name a different context.

The compressor moves through Initialization and Refresh (IR), First Order (FO) and Second Order (SO) states. IR sends complete header information to establish or refresh a context. FO sends updates for changes in the packet pattern. SO sends the shortest headers when the sequence number and learned patterns are enough to reconstruct the rest.

The decompressor has No Context, Static Context and Full Context states. It advances after successful decompression and moves back after repeated failures. These states apply in all three modes: Unidirectional (U), Bidirectional Optimistic (O) and Bidirectional Reliable (R). The mode determines how the two ends move between states and use feedback.

The channel is expected to preserve packet order and not duplicate packets between the compressor and decompressor. ROHC is designed to handle loss and residual errors, meaning errors that lower layers did not detect.
sections.plainLanguage:
For each stream, both ends keep information needed to shorten and rebuild headers. The sender starts by sharing more information, then sends less as the receiver learns the pattern.

The three modes differ in how they use receiver feedback. All modes use the same compressor and decompressor states.

sections.title: Predicting Header Fields
sections.content:
ROHC often sends only the least significant bits (LSBs) of a changing value. The decompressor combines those bits with a reference value that both sides have verified. Window-based LSB encoding keeps several possible references at the compressor, because the compressor may not know which valid reference the decompressor is using.

For RTP, the timestamp often advances by a regular stride. ROHC can send a scaled timestamp, then rebuild the original using the shared stride and offset. When timestamps closely track time, timer-based compression lets the receiver estimate a timestamp from packet arrival time and use the transmitted bits to correct that estimate.

When an IPv4 Identification value usually increases with the RTP sequence number, ROHC can encode their offset rather than the full identifier. If the identifier is random, it is sent as-is. These methods use verified references and checks so that an incorrect value is less likely to become the basis for decoding later packets.
sections.plainLanguage:
Many header values change in a pattern. ROHC sends only enough bits to identify the next value, using an earlier verified value as a reference.

It can also use regular timestamp changes or the relationship between an IP identifier and a sequence number. When a value cannot be predicted, the compressor can send it directly.

sections.title: Contexts, Packet Types and Feedback
sections.content:
A channel is configured with parameters such as the largest CID and the profiles its decompressor accepts. Small CIDs range from 0 to 15; large CIDs range from 0 to 16383. An Initialization and Refresh (IR) packet associates a CID with a profile and can establish the context. An IR-DYN packet can refresh dynamic information, but cannot initialize a context that has not received an IR packet.

A ROHC packet can contain padding, feedback elements, a compressed header and payload. The framework reserves packet-type markers for padding or CID information, feedback, IR-DYN, IR and segments. Other packet types are defined by individual profiles.

The decompressor can send an ACK to report successful decompression, a NACK when dynamic context information is out of sync, or a STATIC-NACK when static context information is missing or invalid. Feedback can travel separately or be carried with packets. Segmentation is provided for occasional large packets, while the RFC recommends using link-layer segmentation when available and suitable.
sections.plainLanguage:
An IR packet tells the receiver which profile to use and can set up the stream's context. Later packets can use shorter forms and refer to that context by its identifier.

The receiver can acknowledge success or report that some or all of its remembered information needs repair. Feedback can be sent on its own or alongside other packets.

sections.title: Recovery and Mode Changes
sections.content:
In U-mode, packets travel from compressor to decompressor without requiring a return channel. The compressor periodically sends context information again and returns to a less compressed state when the header pattern changes. This makes U-mode usable without feedback, though the RFC notes that it is less efficient and somewhat more exposed to loss propagation.

O-mode uses feedback mainly for error-recovery requests. A NACK makes the compressor send updates, and acknowledgments of significant updates are optional. It does not use periodic refreshes. R-mode uses acknowledgments for context updates; the compressor advances only after it receives an acknowledgment, and the decompressor uses only packets with a 7- or 8-bit cyclic redundancy check (CRC) to update its context or as a reference.

All modes use CRCs to check reconstructed headers, though the CRC size and use differ by mode and packet type. After a failed check, the decompressor can try local sequence-number repairs where applicable. Repeated failures can make it fall back to a lower context state and request an update. The decompressor initiates mode changes, and feedback that starts a change must carry a CRC. Returning to U-mode uses a three-message handshake.
sections.plainLanguage:
U-mode works without replies and refreshes context from time to time. O-mode uses replies mainly when the receiver needs an update, while R-mode confirms context updates before the sender relies on them.

Checks help the receiver detect bad reconstructions. If failures continue, it can request fresh context information and reduce how much it assumes.

sections.title: Compressed Headers, Lists and Checks
sections.content:
The RTP profile defines three main compressed packet types. Type 0 carries a sequence number when the receiver already knows the field patterns. Type 1 can carry more sequence-number bits or changes to the timestamp or IP identifier. Type 2 can update parameters for most sequence-number-based field patterns. Extensions carry further values when the base packet type is not enough.

ROHC can also compress ordered lists, such as RTP contributing sources and IP extension headers. It assigns list items indexes, then can send indexes instead of repeating the full items. When a list changes, its encoding can describe the full list or express removals and insertions relative to a reference list.

A CRC checks the header reconstructed by the decompressor against the original header. In compressed headers, the CRC is calculated over the original header before compression. The RFC separates stable and changing header fields during this calculation so that work on stable fields can be reused.
sections.plainLanguage:
Short packet types carry only the changing values the receiver needs. Longer packet types carry updates when the packet pattern changes.

Repeated lists can be sent as indexes, with only the changes described when the list is different. A CRC helps the receiver check whether its rebuilt header matches the original.

sections.title: The Four Profiles
sections.content:
A profile defines how ROHC handles a kind of packet stream. Profile 0x0000 sends IP packets uncompressed, including packets such as IP fragments and RTCP for which compression is unavailable or unsuitable. Profile 0x0001 compresses RTP/UDP/IP. Profile 0x0002 compresses UDP/IP streams that are not RTP and creates a 16-bit sequence number that increases for each packet in the stream.

Profile 0x0003 compresses the IP header chain through the ESP header. It uses the ESP sequence number as its compression basis. When encryption hides headers after ESP, this profile does not try to compress those later headers.

The RFC assigns these four profile identifiers and says future identifiers require a permanent, detailed specification that supports interoperability. The lower eight bits of an identifier have allocation ranges for IETF standards-track and other specifications, while the value 255 is reserved for extensibility.
sections.plainLanguage:
ROHC has separate profiles for RTP traffic, other UDP traffic, ESP traffic and packets sent without compression. Each profile tells the receiver how to read and rebuild that kind of packet.

The RFC also sets rules for assigning identifiers to future profiles so that independent implementations can agree on their meaning.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encryption removes the repeated header information that compression uses. The RFC notes that RTP can encrypt its payload while leaving headers clear, which still permits header compression. ROHC preserves the RTP sequence number and timestamp, so those values can still support payload encryption methods that use them.

A faulty or malicious compressor could cause a decompressor to rebuild a packet that differs from the original while still having valid IP, UDP and RTP headers. The RFC says end-to-end authentication and integrity checks can detect such changes, and ROHC's internal checksum reduces the chance that a mismatch goes unnoticed.

An attacker able to inject false context or feedback packets could reduce compression efficiency. The RFC notes that access to inject arbitrary packets at the link layer creates broader security concerns as well.
sections.plainLanguage: Header compression does not encrypt packet contents or replace end-to-end integrity checks. A false packet could disrupt compression, while authentication and integrity mechanisms can help detect changed data.
